gandhi-ashram-joyag.desc: In late 1946, after communal violence in Noakhali, Mahatma Gandhi walked from village to village to promote peace. He arrived at Joyag in January 1947, and a local landowner donated property that became the Gandhi Ashram Trust. Today the trust runs community development work, and a memorial museum displays photographs, letters and documents from his time in Noakhali.
blocks: How to get there
From Maijdi or Chowmuhani, take a CNG toward Sonaimuri and on to Joyag.
Good to know
Check opening hours locally; the museum may close on some days.

glance: Markets in Hatiya, Subarnachar and Maijdi
noakhali-char-mohisher-doi.desc: Herds of buffalo graze on the chars of Hatiya and Subarnachar, and their thick milk is turned into curd set overnight in clay pots. It is pleasantly sour and very rich, eaten at the end of a meal, with flattened rice and molasses, or simply with a spoon. In Noakhali it is an essential part of wedding and festival feasts.

noakhali-buffalo-bathan.desc: On the newly formed chars of the Meghna estuary, herders keep buffalo in open-range camps called bathan. The animals graze on grass and wade through tidal creeks, while herders live in simple shelters and milk them daily. This old way of life supplies the region's famous curd, and is a striking sight for anyone visiting the islands around Hatiya and Nijhum Dwip.
blocks: Good to know
Ask herders before approaching the animals; buffalo can be protective.

glance: About 10–20 BDT per pitha from street vendors
Winter street stalls in Maijdi and Chowmuhani
noakhali-chitoi-pitha-duck.desc: Chitoi pitha is made from rice-flour batter steamed in small clay moulds over a wood fire, giving a soft centre and a lightly crisp base. In Noakhali and neighbouring districts, a winter favourite is to pair it with rich duck curry cooked with plenty of onion and spices. Street vendors make them fresh in the early morning and evening.

glance: 175 km to Noakhali by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
nijhum-dwip.desc: Nijhum Dwip, the 'silent island', formed from silt in the Meghna estuary and was later planted with mangroves. It is now a national park, and the spotted deer introduced decades ago have multiplied into large herds. Early mornings at the forest edge or along tidal creeks are the best chance to see them, along with waders and migratory birds in winter. The island has a few simple resorts and guesthouses.
blocks: How to get there
Reach Hatiya by launch from Dhaka or by boat from Noakhali's Chairman Ghat, cross Hatiya by motorbike to Moktaria Ghat, then a short boat ride to Nijhum Dwip.
Good to know
Plan for at least one night. Avoid the monsoon months when the sea is rough and launches may be cancelled; follow weather signals. Bring cash and a torch.

bajra-shahi-mosque.desc: The Bajra Shahi Mosque was built in the 18th century, during the Mughal period, and is among the best-preserved mosques of that era in the region. It has three domes and an elegant facade, set on a raised platform overlooking a wide pond. It is still in use and protected as a heritage site.
blocks: How to get there
On the Sonaimuri side of the Chowmuhani–Cumilla road; a CNG from Chowmuhani takes about 30 minutes.
Good to know
Avoid prayer times and dress modestly.

musapur-closure.desc: The Musapur closure is a regulator dam on the Little Feni (Choto Feni) river near the coast in Companiganj. Planted trees along the embankment, a wide estuary view and fishing boats make it a popular local escape, especially at sunset. It is far less known outside the district.
blocks: How to get there
From Basurhat (Companiganj), take a CNG or easy-bike to Musapur.
Good to know
Stay off the sluice structures and avoid visiting in storm or high-tide warnings.

glance: 175 km to Noakhali by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
ramzan-mia-mosque.desc: The Ramzan Mia Jame Mosque, known locally as the Chowdhury Mosque, stands in Batoiya union of Kabirhat upazila. It is believed to date from the Mughal period, roughly 300 years ago, and was founded by Shaykh Nurullah Chowdhury and Shaykh Mujir Ali Chowdhury, whose descendants still look after it. Its three domes once carried fine decorative work, much of which is now fading for lack of care. It is a quiet stop for anyone interested in Noakhali's older villages.
blocks: How to get there
From Maijdee (Noakhali town) take a CNG to Kabirhat, then on to Batoiya union; ask for the Chowdhury Mosque.
Good to know
Visit outside prayer times and dress modestly.

glance: 175 km to Noakhali by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
hatiya-island.desc: Hatiya is an old island upazila at the mouth of the Meghna, and the stepping stone to Nijhum Dwip. Its villages are surrounded by paddy fields, ponds and coconut palms, and its ghats bustle with fishing boats and launches. Riding across the island by motorbike gives a feel for coastal farming and fishing life that most visitors never see.
blocks: How to get there
Launch from Dhaka's Sadarghat (overnight) or sea truck/boat from Chairman Ghat in Noakhali.
Good to know
Crossings depend on weather; do not travel during storm signals. Wear a life jacket on small boats.

glance: Fish ghats on Hatiya island such as Chairman Ghat, and local rice hotels on the island
hatiya-ilish-nona-ilish.desc: Hatiya island sits where the Meghna meets the Bay of Bengal, and in season trawlers unload hilsa at ghats like Chairman Ghat. Islanders eat it fresh, fried in its own oil or in a light curry. They also make nona ilish: the fish is cut without washing, packed in clay pots between thick layers of salt and kept for months, then rinsed and cooked as a very salty, pungent curry or fry. Fresh hilsa is most plentiful in the monsoon and early autumn; fishing stops during the October breeding-season ban.
